name: Bole
lede: Bole is a fine red-brown clay or ochre, best known as the smooth base laid under gold leaf, and a word that has meant several different earths.

sections.title: A red earth for gilding
sections.body:
Bole is an iron-rich earth, red in most of its uses, that was valued where a surface had to take a very high polish, above all as the base under gold leaf [1]. Paterson's dictionary calls it an orange-red or reddish-brown earth color from the unctuous clays of the same name [2]. The color ground of a painting, the prepared layer that makes a surface less absorbent, could be bole or gesso [2].

Pigment sources recognize white boles and red boles, and the word has never named one single material [1]. The books do not trace where the word itself comes from.

sections.title: Armenian, red and white
sections.body:
Armenian bole was a deep red ochre found originally in Cappadocia, according to Field in 1835 [3]. It was the variety used as a base for gilding [4]. Red bole is a different thing in geology: a soft red clay formed by weathering on the surfaces of lava flows, which includes impure halloysite, a mineral named after O. d'Halloy (1707-89) [5]. White bole is simply a name for kaolin, the china clay [6].

Books disagree about what the plain word means. Weber and Bristow treat bole and bolus as synonyms for red ochre [4]. Harley found in seventeenth-century British sources that bole occasionally meant red ochre, but more often meant Armenian bole, "bole Armoniack", which de Mayerne records in the priming of canvas [1]. Terry, writing in 1893, used bole for the chestnut-colored grade of Tuscan sienna earth, and Weber called it the typical sienna [7]. Terry's trade grades for it, in falling quality, were boletta, fascia, cerchione and terra guilla [7].

sections.title: Where bole turns up
sections.body:
In 1703-04 the Cambridge chemist John Francis Vigani put together a collection of nearly 700 samples of materia medica, and it includes an Armenian bole beside red ochre and vermilion [8]. By 1869 a bookbinders' preparation called assiette, used on page edges before gilding, was a mix of one pound of Armenian bole with 2 ounces each of bloodstone and galena [9]. Green earth was recommended as an alternative base for gilding when red bole was not wanted [10].

Medieval Latin texts used *brunus* for a brown earth [11]. Brunello reads it as an iron- and manganese-rich ochre like umber or sienna, and says it may have been the same as bole, while Thompson found the word in a fourteenth-century manuscript and suggested it could be bole used as a pigment [11]. Related red earths have local histories: a letters patent of 1626 gave control of the Forest of Dean's "Spanish Browne" and "Almagro", and Carrillo reports an almagre mine near Questa, New Mexico, worked in prehistoric times [12].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here is a moderate reddish brown, within a color distance (ΔE) of 1.6 of an ISCC-NBS 1955 block of that name [13]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary pictures the color on plate 6 and dates its first record to 1386 [13]. That is a dictionary color, one red-brown out of a family that ran from white clay through red to chestnut [1][6][13]. Fresh bole sold for gilding would not necessarily look like this on a screen.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, a color within ΔE 6 of this swatch covers at least 5% of the canvas in 895 paintings, 3.8% of the archive [14]. The decade 1450 stands out, with 27 of 109 paintings (25%, 6.6 times the museums' baseline) [14]. By role, it is a mid-tone in 65% of those paintings and a shadow in 30% [14].

The country that carries it most is Tibet, in 15 of 47 paintings (32%), followed by Nepal in 4 of 25 [14]. The strongest matches include [[painting:cma-136332|Vajradhara, Nairatmya, and mahasiddhas Virupa and Kanha]], a Tibetan painting of about 1450, and the Teotihuacan [[painting:aic-14968|mural fragment of a maguey ritual]] [14]. Clay in this family does turn up there: metahalloysite has been tentatively identified in late seventeenth-century Tibetan thangkas, though in a white pigment role and not as bole [5]. Among painters, Dürer has it in 7 of 47 works and Munch in 7 of 50 [14].

It keeps the company of [[brick]], [[mahogany]], [[terracotta]] and [[sienna]] [14]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike color and not proof of any clay [14].

questions.q: Why was bole used under gold leaf?
choices: It gave a smooth surface that could be polished to a high shine
It was the only red pigment
questions.answer: It gave a smooth surface that could be polished to a high shine

questions.q: Bole always meant one and the same red earth.
Which material is called white bole?

openers: Armenian bole was the red earth that went under gold leaf; white bole was just china clay.
Look for a red-brown showing through worn gilding on an old frame or icon: that is the bole beneath.
